# Plugin developer guide

<!-- Generated by `uv run python -m engine.plugin_guide` from the host's code. Do not edit by hand. -->

Plugin API **0.3.79**. Declare `plugin_api: '>=0.3,<0.4'` in the manifest: 0.x minor versions may break, so a manifest for an earlier minor version is refused. This guide is generated from the code and is the contract; names here are the names in the code. `docs/plugin-api-0.x.md` says what changed in each version.

The public plugin contract: the only module a plugin imports from the host.

A plugin is a Python package with a `plugin.yaml` beside it. At startup the host reads the manifest, validates the plugin's settings, and calls its entry function with a `Registrar`. What the plugin registers must match the manifest's `provides` and `subscribes` exactly; registration is all or nothing.

Plugins change knowledge only through ops, which the applier checks, records in the ledger and can undo. Ops get a writer limited to what they declare; validators, stage checks and event handlers get read-only views; person actions return a proposal the person reviews. Plugins read core records and their own, never another plugin's. Every identifier is namespaced `<plugin>/<name>`.

Plugins run in the host's process: enabling one trusts its code. A plugin that breaks its contract, or whose callback raises an unexpected exception, is turned off for the run with the reason in its status; core work and other plugins carry on. Today lines, interface items, event handlers and jobs are contained per call: a failing call is skipped and noted, and the plugin is turned off only after `workspace.plugins.failures_before_off` failures in a row there.

To try a plugin without touching a real workspace, run `cockpit demo --plugin <its folder>`: it makes (or reuses) a demo workspace of made-up data, links the plugin folder into it, turns the plugin on and serves it. Edits show after a restart; `--fresh` starts the demo over, and an installed plugin is named instead of its folder.

For a plugin's own tests, install the host from its repository without the web screens, which need npm to build: `PM_COCKPIT_WITHOUT_SCREENS=1 uv pip install "pm-cockpit @ git+<the host's repository address>@<branch or tag>"`. Test connectors with `engine.plugin_api.testing` (see Connectors), never the host's internals.

One distribution may ship several plugins. They may share a helper package of their own (a module neither plugin registers from); what a plugin may not do is import another plugin's registered package or read its records.

Import everything from `engine.plugin_api`: `ConnectorError`, `retry_after`, `Poll`, `SourceItem`, `ItemFile`, `ExtractError`, `EventDetails`, `MessageDetails`, `PLUGIN_API_VERSION`, `Settings`, `Record`, `OpModel`, `EvidenceIn`, `ANY`, `NeedsPerson`, `PluginMisuse`, `RefTo`, `InList`, `Tier`, `WriteContext`, `Stored`, `StoreError`, `ReadView`, `OpWriter`, `EventContext`, `ActionContext`, `LintFinding`, `TakeBack`, `WorkingCopyContext`, `InterfaceItem`, `TodayLine`, `CORE_LINE_ACTIONS`, `PacketContext`, `LongText`, `Unit`, `Part`, `KnowledgeParts`, `PacketParts`, `Proposal`, `NewFile`, `Preview`, `Choice`, `Group`, `Item`, `Registrar`, `StageDefinition`, `StageCheckResult`, `StageStatus`, `SetupState`, `ToolBox`, `ToolResult`, `ToolError`. Nothing else in the host is an API.

## The manifest: plugin.yaml

A plugin's manifest, `plugin.yaml`, beside its package. It is read and checked before any plugin code is imported: unknown keys are errors, and what the code registers must match `provides` and `subscribes` exactly.

| Key | Type | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | str | required | The plugin's name and the namespace of its ids. |
| `version` | str | required | The plugin's own version. |
| `plugin_api` | str | required | The plugin API versions it works with, e.g. '>=0.3,<0.4'. |
| `description` | str | required | One line saying what the plugin is for. |
| `depends_on` | list[Dependency] | `[]` | Plugins that must be enabled first. |
| `depends_on[].name` | str | required | The other plugin's name; it must be enabled too. |
| `depends_on[].version` | str | required | A version range the other plugin must satisfy, such as '>=1.0,<2'. |
| `interfaces` | Interfaces | see below | How it works with other plugins, only through the core. |
| `interfaces.defines` | list[str] | `[]` | Interfaces this plugin defines, by name. |
| `interfaces.provides` | list[str] | `[]` | Interfaces this plugin provides, as "<plugin>/<name>@<major>". |
| `interfaces.uses` | list[InterfaceUse] | `[]` | Interfaces this plugin reads or requests. |
| `interfaces.uses[].interface` | str | required | The interface and the oldest version that works: "<name>@<major>" or "<name>@<major>.<minor>". |
| `interfaces.uses[].optional` | bool | `False` | The plugin still works when no enabled plugin provides it. |
| `subscribes` | list[str \| Subscription] | `[]` | Events the plugin handles: a name, or {event, kinds}. |
| `subscribes[].event` | str | required | One of the events listed under Events. |
| `subscribes[].kinds` | list[str] | `[]` | Only records of these kinds (file kinds for file.added); empty means every kind. |
| `provides` | Provides | see below | Everything the plugin registers, by id. |
| `provides.record_types` | list[str] | `[]` | Record kinds the plugin registers. |
| `provides.stages` | list[str] | `[]` | Own record kinds the plugin gives default stages. |
| `provides.stage_checks` | list[str] | `[]` | Stage entry checks the plugin registers. |
| `provides.ops` | list[str] | `[]` | Ops the plugin registers. |
| `provides.op_validators` | list[str] | `[]` | Core or own ops the plugin registers a validator for. |
| `provides.ai_task_kinds` | list[str] | `[]` | AI task kinds the plugin registers. |
| `provides.file_kinds` | list[str] | `[]` | File kinds the plugin registers. |
| `provides.actions` | list[str] | `[]` | Person actions the plugin registers. |
| `provides.lints` | list[str] | `[]` | Lints the plugin registers. |
| `provides.text_formats` | list[str] | `[]` | Long text formats the plugin registers. |
| `provides.working_copies` | list[str] | `[]` | Working-copy formats the plugin registers. |
| `provides.extractors` | list[str] | `[]` | Readers that turn files of some media types into text. |
| `provides.derived_files` | list[str] | `[]` | Files the plugin generates from its records into each project's folder. |
| `provides.panels` | list[str] | `[]` | Screens listing records, described as data. |
| `provides.today` | list[str] | `[]` | Contributors of lines on Today. |
| `provides.jobs` | list[str] | `[]` | Work run on a schedule while the app runs. |
| `provides.setup_steps` | list[str] | `[]` | Steps added to the first-run setup. |
| `provides.data_forms` | list[str] | `[]` | Kinds of data file the screens offer a form for, checked by a schema. |
| `provides.connectors` | list[str] | `[]` | Places the assistant can keep reading. |
| `provides.connector_reads` | dict[str, Literal['mail', 'calendar']] | `{}` | What each of the plugin's connectors reads, by connector: mail or calendar. The setup walkthrough offers an add-on that signs in and reads mail or a calendar as a service to connect, also before it is installed. A connector left out is told apart by its name. |
| `provides.triage_matchers` | list[str] | `[]` | Rule kinds for triaging watched changes. |
| `provides.scorers` | list[str] | `[]` | Deterministic scorers for what only the plugin can judge, which a case in its evaluation folder names with `score:`. |
| `provides.value_lists` | list[str] | `[]` | Value lists the plugin's record fields take their values from. |
| `provides.sign_ins` | list[str] | `[]` | Sign-ins to a service, through its own sign-in page, as the person. |
| `provides.help` | list[str] | `[]` | Help files the plugin ships (Markdown, one section per ## heading, paths relative to its manifest) that asking the assistant reads and cites, like the user guide. Only ## sections are read: text before the first ## heading is left out. |
| `provides.wording` | list[str] | `[]` | Wording files the plugin ships (YAML maps from a wording key to its text, paths relative to its manifest): what the screens call the plugin's own kinds, e.g. stages.group.<plugin>/<kind>. Every key names something in the plugin's namespace; the workspace's ui.wording overrides any of them. |
| `provides.playbook` | str \| None | `None` | The plugin's own playbook. Not yet available. |
| `provides.evals` | str \| None | `None` | A folder beside plugin.yaml holding the plugin's own evaluation cases, in the core's format; `cockpit evaluate` runs them while the plugin is enabled. |
| `provides.data` | str \| None | `None` | A folder beside plugin.yaml holding the data files the plugin ships (templates, word lists); the workspace overrides them in plugin-data/<plugin>/ and per project in plugin-data/<plugin>/projects/<id>/. |
| `config_schema` | str | required | module:Class of the plugin's Settings subclass. |
| `requires` | Requires | see below | What the plugin may reach and needs. |
| `requires.network` | list[str] | `[]` | Hosts the plugin's connectors may reach through the core's web client ("api.example.com", "*.example.com"); nothing else is reachable. |
| `requires.secrets` | list[str] | `[]` | Names of the secrets the plugin may read (a key, a sign-in token): set per workspace in workspace.plugins.secrets, or kept on this computer by the plugin itself. |
| `requires.data_levels` | list[Literal['open', 'internal', 'restricted']] | `['open', 'internal']` | Every data level the plugin's record types and file kinds use, the default internal included. |
| `requires.tools` | list[Tool] | `[]` | Outside programs the plugin runs. |
| `requires.tools[].name` | str | required | The program's name: how it is found on the PATH and how its probe starts. |
| `requires.tools[].min_version` | str | required | The oldest version that works; empty accepts any version. |
| `requires.tools[].probe` | str | required | A command that prints the version, starting with the name, e.g. 'renderer --version'. |
| `requires.tools[].optional` | bool | `False` | Missing is allowed: the plugin runs and the features listed turn off. |
| `requires.tools[].features` | list[str] | `[]` | What turns off without it, in plain words. |
| `entry` | str | required | module:function called with the Registrar at startup. |

### Not yet available

A non-empty value for any of these keys turns the plugin off with the reason.

| Key | For |
|---|---|
| `provides.playbook` | a plugin's own playbook |

## Settings

Base for a plugin's settings, read from `config/plugins/<plugin>.yaml`. Every field needs a default and a description; unknown keys are refused. Handlers and actions get a copy as `context.config`. A field may be a nested model (shown as its own section on the Settings screen; keep it to one level) and may use an alias when its name in the file can't be a Python name.

| Field | Type | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | Literal[1] | `1` | Settings format version. |

## Registering

A staging registry: the host installs it only after checking the manifest. `register(registrar)` may read `registrar.config` (the plugin's settings, already checked) to decide what to register; registration is fixed until the app restarts. The app never restarts on its own: a change to a plugin's settings, or turning plugins on or off, makes it say a restart is needed and hold new AI work until the person chooses "Restart now". Until then the plugin keeps the settings it registered with and isn't told of the change. Data the workspace adds later (its own lists, profiles) is read per call, not at registration.

#### `registrar.record_type(model: type[Record]) -> None`

Register a record kind: a `Record` subclass with `record_kind` ("<plugin>/<name>") and an id `prefix` (capital letters, unique in the workspace).

#### `registrar.op(model: type[OpModel], tier: Tier, apply: Callable, *, notes: bool = False, candidates: Callable | None = None) -> None`

Register an op: an `OpModel` subclass with a single literal `op` id and a `writes` class variable mapping own record kinds to the fields it may change (`("*",)` to create or delete). `tier` is "data" or "system" (system ops from the assistant wait for the person). `apply(op, writer, settings)` makes the change through the `OpWriter`; raising StoreError refuses this op only. With `notes=True` the op is also offered to the core's reading of notes, so the assistant can use it on what the person hands in: give it an `EvidenceIn` field, which the core checks against the input, for anything it claims. It is offered only when the note's data level covers every record type the op writes, so a note handed in as internal never writes restricted records. `candidates(view, settings[, project]) -> list[(id, name)]` lists records such an op may name (with a third argument, it gets the id of the project the note was handed in for, or None), shown to the run (at most 50, at the level of the record types the op writes), so it can refer to an existing one by id. With None the person named no project: list what the note could be about across the workspace, most likely first (recently changed, still open), since only the first 50 reach the run; an empty list leaves the run nothing to name, so it can only create.

#### `registrar.op_validator(op_name: str, fn: Callable) -> None`

Check a core or own op before it applies: `fn(op, view, origin)` (or `fn(op, view)`; `origin` may also be keyword-only) returns a list of refusal messages, empty to let it through. The view is the changeset so far. `origin` is {"actor": "pm" | "assistant" | "rule" | "plugin", "trust": "trusted" | "untrusted", "via": "screen" | "note" | "input" | "task" | "rule" | "action" | "handler" | "job", "task": the run's task kind, "about": the record it works on as {"kind", "id"} or None, "request": the run's request id or None, "part": the part of the record the request names (as given to `queue_request(part=)`) or None}; ops a plugin's event handler or job staged with `apply_op` have actor "plugin" and via "handler" or "job". A validator with a parameter named `settings` (or `**kwargs`) also gets the plugin's settings by keyword, so a check that depends on a setting is a validator, and its refusal is fed back in a fix round like any other; a refusal raised from an op's `apply` refuses the op without a fix round. Before anything applies, the core dry-runs the whole changeset in order (text writes included) and rolls it back, so a validator sees what earlier ops in it created; with the check at the write boundary, a validator usually runs about three times per op, so it must be pure and quick. There is no cache the core keeps for a pass: the view is made anew for each call. Cache costly derived data by its content (a hash of the text it comes from, say, in a module-level dictionary of bounded size), never by record id or version alone, since the changeset so far may change what a version holds.

#### `registrar.task_kind(name: str, *, ops: tuple[str, ...] = (), label: str = '', output: str = 'ops', field: str | None = None, anchored: bool = False, questions: int = 0, where: dict[str, Any] | None = None, start_where: dict[str, Any] | None = None, role: str = 'write', prompt: str = 'notes', playbook: str = 'notes', on: str | None = None, packet: Callable | None = None, tier: str | None = None, max_output: int | None = None, expected_output: int | None = None, temperature: float | None = None, all_or_nothing: bool = False, requires_ops: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = (), learning: str = 'core') -> None`

Register AI work: the core or own ops its answer may use, and `label`, what to call it on screen.

`prompt` names the instructions: a core prompt ("notes") or the plugin's own, "<plugin>/<name>", read from `prompts/<name>.md` in the plugin's folder. `playbook` names its guidance the same way, from `guidance/<name>.md`. The workspace overrides a plugin's prompt with `prompts/<plugin>/<name>.md`.

`on` is the record kind a run is about (core or own), when it works on one record: the request then carries that record, and the person can start it from the record. `packet(target, view, settings, note) -> PacketParts` says what the run sees (without it, the run sees what reading notes sees); `view` is a PacketContext, whose `origin` says who started the run. It runs before every call, so it must be deterministic and quick; raising StoreError stops the run with that message for the person: the request waits with it as the reason, and no retry, fix round or escalation follows. `where` narrows which records of kind `on` the work is offered on and may start on: {field: value} or {field: (value, ...)}, every field matching; ANY means the field has a value and None that it has none, which for a long text field asks whether the record has text in it. `start_where`, in the same form, narrows further only the runs the person starts (from a record, or offered to them there): requests a plugin, an action or a stage queues, and any request naming a `part`, check `where` alone, so a kind the person starts only on an empty record can still continue part by part. The packet's `max_output` hint is never below 256 tokens.

`output` is "ops" (the answer is a changeset of `ops`) or "draft": the answer is plain prose for the long text field `field` of the record the run is about (`on` is required). The core wraps it as a pending `text.draft` version for the person's review, runs lints on it (lints on the op "text.draft"), sends a "return" finding back for one fix round, and continues a draft cut off at the output limit once before holding it. With `anchored=True` the draft revises the current text: the run sees it with an id on each unit, starts every paragraph it writes with the ids it came from, and a core check refuses a draft that leaves a unit unaccounted for, names an unknown id, or splits or merges an atomic unit; the paragraph map is kept with the version. The core adds the text with its ids after the packet's parts, as untrusted material: ids are p1, p2, ... in the order of the field format's units over the whole text, so a packet can name the same ids. A request's `part` limits a draft to a span or a place in the text (see `queue_request`). `questions=N` lets a draft end with up to N questions for the person, in a `<questions>` block the core takes off the text and keeps on the version (`questions`), shown beside it; more than N gets a fix round. In an anchored answer the `Removed:` line comes before the `<questions>` block, which is always last.

`role` is "write" (the default: work that writes or changes things), "check" (an independent second opinion on work already done) or "research" (gathering from sources). The workspace maps roles to tiers (`ai.roles`). A check never runs on an account that wrote the record it is about (its accepted and pending text versions and the changes AI runs made to it), unless the person accepts the same account for checks; the run then records which kind of independence it had (`Run.independence`). With no account to take it, the check waits for the person and says why. The packet decides what a check sees: give it the work, never the writing run's own material.

`tier`, `max_output` (the most tokens an answer may use), `expected_output` (typical answer size, for estimates before there are past runs) and `temperature` are defaults; the workspace's `ai.tasks.<kind>` overrides them.

`all_or_nothing=True` applies an answer's ops together: if any is refused, none applies, and the changeset is recorded as refused with each op's reason, for ops that depend on each other (notes that summarize findings made in the same answer). Ops held for the person still wait as usual.

`requires_ops` names ops (from `ops`) an answer must include at least one of, for work whose every answer reports (findings, or an explicit "nothing found"): an answer with none of them is refused like any invariant, which gets the usual fix round, then a stronger tier; one still without them is held for the person as refused.

`learning` is "core" (the default) or "own". With "own" the core's learning from inputs, new-term scan, first-name resolution against people and fact ranking into the workspace's facts don't run on this work, and a run's knowledge section (`view.knowledge`) leaves out facts. A task kind working `on` a record type that declares `learning = "own"` is treated the same.

#### `registrar.stage_check(id: str, fn: Callable) -> None`

Register a pure check: (record, read_view, settings) -> StageCheckResult. Never call AI. When several checks refuse a move, their reasons are shown joined with "; ", so write each as a short clause that reads well beside others.

#### `registrar.stages(record_type: str, stages: list[StageDefinition | dict], *, moves=None) -> None`

Default stages for one of this plugin's record types. The workspace's stages.yaml may replace them. `moves` is "person" (the default: only the person moves items) or "rule" (stage checks move items forward).

#### `registrar.file_kind(name: str, *, details: type[BaseModel] | None = None, accept: tuple[str, ...] = (), max_mb: float | None = None, label: str = '', data_level: str | None = None) -> None`

Declare what a kind of file is for: the details asked for when one is added (a pydantic model), the media types it accepts (within the workspace's), and a size cap (never above the workspace's). `data_level` ("open", "internal" or "restricted"; default internal) is the level a file added under this kind gets when the person doesn't choose one at the upload; a level the manifest's `requires.data_levels` doesn't list refuses the plugin. A person's explicit choice at the upload stands, and only the person changes it afterwards.

#### `registrar.action(name: str, *, label: str, run: Callable, on: str | None = None, file_kinds: tuple[str, ...] = (), where: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> None`

Something the person starts: on a record of kind `on` (core or own; "file" with optional `file_kinds`), or on the workspace when `on` is None. `where` narrows the records of kind `on` it is offered on and may run on, as for task kinds: {field: value} or {field: (value, ...)}, every field matching. `run(target, context, choices) -> Proposal` is deterministic work (it may run declared programs through `context.tools`); the person reviews the proposal, and what they approve applies as theirs. Raising StoreError or ToolError shows its message to the person; any other exception turns the plugin off.

#### `registrar.text_format(name: str, units: Callable) -> None`

A long text format: `units(text) -> list[Unit]`, spans that cover the text exactly, in order, each with a kind and whether it is atomic (never split or merged). Pure and deterministic; the core checks the coverage. The core ships "plain" (blank-line paragraphs) and "markdown" (its blocks).

#### `registrar.working_copy(name: str, *, label: str, extension: str, media_type: str, hand_out: Callable, take_back: Callable, text_formats: tuple[str, ...] = ()) -> None`

A file format people edit long text in with their own tools. `hand_out(text, context) -> bytes` makes the file from a version; `take_back(data, base_text, context) -> TakeBack` reads a file back, given the text of the version it was handed out from. Both are deterministic, with no AI; anything take_back can't map goes in `unmapped`, never dropped. Handing out an untouched file and taking it back must give the same text: the core reads every file back as it hands it out, and refuses to hand out one that doesn't. A returned file becomes a `text.propose` made from the handed-out version, so the review is three-way when the text moved on. `text_formats` limits it to long text in those formats (empty: any). The media type must be one the workspace accepts (storage.files.accepted_types).

#### `registrar.extractor(name: str, *, label: str, media_types: Sequence[str], extract: Callable) -> None`

A reader that turns files of some media types into text (listed in `provides.extractors`), for the attachments a connector hands over and for `view.file_text`. `extract(data, name) -> str | None` gets the file's bytes and its file name and returns its text; return None to decline a file, which the core's own reader (if it has one for the type) then reads. Raise `ExtractError(reason)` with the reason in plain words when the file can't be read (locked, damaged): the person is told it wasn't read and why. An empty text is the same as that. Plugins' readers are asked before the core's own, in plugin name order, and the core cuts the text at the configured size. `label` names the kind of file on screen (`Reading <label> isn't working: …`). Deterministic, quick and offline: it never calls AI or the network, and it never follows a path the file names.

#### `registrar.define_interface(name: str, *, version: str, item: type[BaseModel], events: dict[str, type[BaseModel]] | None = None, task_kinds: tuple[str, ...] = ()) -> None`

Define a versioned interface other plugins provide or use (listed in `interfaces.defines`): `item` is the pydantic model of one item, `events` the events providers raise with their payload models, and `task_kinds` the work a provider may offer for others to request. `version` is "<major>.<minor>": add only optional fields within a major version, and bump the major to change anything else. A plugin that defines an interface may also provide and use it.

#### `registrar.provide_interface(interface: str, *, items: Callable, task_kinds: dict[str, str] | None = None, about: Callable | None = None) -> None`

Provide an interface ("<name>@<major>", listed in `interfaces.provides`), defined here or by another plugin. `items(view, settings, project) -> list[dict]` returns what this plugin offers through it: for one project when `project` is an id, everything when it is None (a function taking only `view, settings` is called for everything and filtered). Each item is checked against the definition when read; include `project` (an id) for items that belong to one, and `data_level` when it isn't "internal". It must be quick and deterministic. `task_kinds` maps the interface's task kind names to this plugin's own task kinds, so others can request them. `about(view, settings, item) -> record | (kind, id) | None` says which of this plugin's records an item (as `items` returned it) stands for, so a user can request work on the item itself; the record must be of the kind the requested task kind is `on`. A function taking a fourth argument also gets the interface's task name being requested, so different task kinds can work on different records. Raise the interface's events from an op with `writer.emit`, or from an event handler with `context.emit`. With no plugin defining the interface running, nothing reads it.

#### `registrar.today(name: str, *, lines: Callable) -> None`

Lines for the Today list (listed in `provides.today`): `lines(view, settings) -> list[TodayLine]`, called whenever Today is shown, so it must be quick and deterministic and never call AI. A line's `action` is one of this plugin's person actions or task kinds, or one of the core's own (`CORE_LINE_ACTIONS`), which need `about`: "go" a `request` waiting for the go, "answer" a `question`, "move-stage" a record of a kind with stages, and "open" or "review" any record. A line that counts several items ("three runs wait for your go") names the one record its button acts on as `about`; when no single record fits, use "open" on the most relevant one, or leave `action` unset and let the line inform. A line naming a core action with the wrong `about` fails the contributor like any bad line.

#### `registrar.panel(name: str, *, title: str, kind: str, columns: tuple[str, ...], view: str = 'table', filter: dict[str, Any] | None = None, primary_action: str | None = None, row_actions: tuple[str, ...] = (), tab: str = 'work', new_action: str | None = None, computed: dict[str, Callable] | None = None, show_for: Callable | None = None) -> None`

A screen listing records (listed in `provides.panels`), described as data so it looks and behaves like the core's (design 7.2): the records of `kind` (core or own) whose fields equal `filter`, shown as `view` ("list", "table" or "board"; a board groups by the first column) with `columns` (fields of the kind, or names in `computed`). `primary_action` is the one action on a row and `row_actions` the rest, in its menu: this plugin's person actions or task kinds on that kind. `new_action` is a person action of this plugin's on the workspace (`on` None) shown above the rows, to add one. Rows are read through the core, and actions run as they always do.

`computed` adds columns that aren't fields: {"words": fn} where `fn(record, view, settings)` returns a short str, a number, a bool or None (a word count, a stage, "complete for its tier", the last build). A computed column can't be named like a field of the kind (that is a load error). It must be quick and deterministic and never call AI; one that raises shows an empty cell and counts as the plugin failing (failure containment). A function taking a fourth argument gets a dict shared by every cell of one listing, to keep work it would otherwise repeat per row (an index of builds by record); it is new for each listing.

Filtered by project, a kind with no `project` field follows its `layout_project` reference: a record is in the project its referenced record is in. `show_for(project, view) -> bool` lists the panel only on the projects it returns True for (a panel of what a parent project's children share, say); without it the panel is on every project.

#### `registrar.document(name: str, *, title: str, render: Callable, tab: str = 'work', show_for: Callable | None = None) -> None`

A read-only document panel (listed in `provides.panels`): a page the plugin composes from many records (a start-here page, a beat sheet, a timeline). `render(view, settings, project) -> str | None` returns Markdown, built per call from the view (`project` is the record of the project in view, as `show_for` gets it, or None for the workspace); None shows that there is nothing to show yet. It must be quick and deterministic and never call AI; one that raises shows the panel's problem and counts as the plugin failing (failure containment).

The screens draw a small Markdown subset as their own elements, never HTML: headings (`#` to `###`), paragraphs, bullet and numbered lists (one level), tables (a header row, then `|---|`), rules (`---`), and inline `**strong**`, `*emphasis*`, `` `code` `` and links. `[text](record:<kind>/<id>)` links to a record the plugin may read (core or its own; one that doesn't exist shows as its text) and opens its page; `[text](https://...)` links to a page outside, shown with its real domain. Anything else, raw HTML included, shows as the characters it is. Up to 200,000 characters. `show_for(project, view) -> bool` lists it only on some projects, as for record panels.

#### `registrar.data_form(name: str, *, label: str, folder: str, schema: type[BaseModel], description: str = '', pattern: str = '*.yaml', single: bool = False) -> None`

A kind of data file the person edits through a form (listed in `provides.data_forms`): the files in `folder` of the plugin's data layers (`view.data`) that match `pattern`, each checked against `schema` (a pydantic model; every field needs a default and a description, as in `Settings`). `pattern` is a glob relative to the folder, ending in `.yaml`, with at most one level of subfolder: `*.yaml` (the default), `*/item.yaml` (one folder per item, beside its own files) or `stages.yaml`. With `single=True` the form is that one file (`pattern` names it): it is listed even before it exists, and no other file can be made.

The screens list the files with the layer each comes from (shipped, the workspace's, a project's) and any problem each has, checked as the plugin's loader would and with defaults checked too (a required value left empty shows). They offer a form built from the schema, as for settings: editing a shipped file saves a copy in the workspace's layer (or a project's), never the shipped one; a new file starts from the schema's defaults or from another file of the kind ("start from"); a copy can be removed to fall back to the less specific one. A save writes only the keys the file already had plus those the person set, never the whole model with its defaults, so keys left out stay left out (a template's `extends` keeps following its base). Every save is checked against the schema (a refusal names the field, or says the file's own rule when the model's validator refused it) and offers Undo. The list shows each file's first problem; opening the file shows the form with it. The plugin reads the files as before, with `view.data(path, project=...)`, and must read them with this same schema: a key left out of a file takes the schema's default, so a loader with other defaults (or a field it requires that the form defaults) sees a different file than the form checked.

#### `registrar.job(name: str, *, every_minutes: int, run: Callable) -> None`

Work on a schedule (listed in `provides.jobs`): `run(context)` with an `EventContext`, every `every_minutes` by default; the workspace changes it or turns the job off in `workspace.plugins.jobs.<name>`. Like an event handler it reads, queues requests, files questions, raises interface events and stages its own ops; it never writes records directly and never calls AI itself. It runs only while the app runs, and each run is recorded.

#### `registrar.connector(name: str, *, label: str, settings: type[BaseModel], poll: Callable, reads: "Literal['mail', 'calendar'] | None" = None) -> None`

A place the assistant can keep reading (listed in `provides.connectors`). A workspace watches it by naming it in `watch.yaml` with its settings, which `settings` (a pydantic model) checks. `poll(settings, state, context) -> Poll` lists what the source holds now as `SourceItem`s (a stable key, a title, the text, who changed it last) and returns the `state` to keep for the next read; set `complete=False` when it lists only what changed. An item can carry files (`SourceItem.files`, `ItemFile`: name, media type, bytes), such as a mail's attachments: the core reads them as text and adds it to the item's text, so the connector never parses a file and a change in a file is a change in the item. Raise `ConnectorError(kind, detail)` with kind `auth`, `no_access`, `not_found`, `outage`, `offline` or `throttled` (with `retry_after=` seconds). The core compares, keeps snapshots and hands in what is new, changed or gone (for a read that lists only changes, the keys in `Poll.removed`); the connector never writes records. `context.web` (when `requires.network` lists hosts) reaches only those hosts, over HTTPS: `context.web.get(url, params=..., headers=...)` and `.post(...)` return a response with `status`, `headers`, `content`, `.text` and `.json()`, and raise `ConnectorError` for no connection (offline), timeouts and 5xx (outage), 401 (auth), 403 (no_access), 404 (not_found), and 429 or 503 with a Retry-After (throttled, with the wait). Those errors carry the answer's `status`, `headers` and `body` (`err.json()`), so a connector can read the service's own error code and raise a better kind: a 403 that means "slow down" is `throttled`, with `retry_after=retry_after(err.headers)`. Every other status (410, say) comes back as a response to read, so a service whose expired change marker is a 404 is caught as `not_found` and one whose marker is a 410 is a status to check; both mean "start over with a full read". A throttled read isn't counted as a failure, and the source isn't read again before its wait ends. `context.secret(name)` reads a secret named in `requires.secrets` (None when it isn't set), `context.keep_secret(name, value)` keeps one on this computer, and `context.access_token(name)` gives a current token for one of the plugin's sign-ins. Test a connector with `engine.plugin_api.testing`. `reads="mail"` or `reads="calendar"` says what the connector reads, so the setup walkthrough offers its add-on as a mail or calendar service, also before it is installed. Say it in the manifest too, as `provides.connector_reads: {<connector>: mail}`, which the registration must match. A connector that says nothing is told apart by its name (mail, mailbox, email or inbox; calendar), and the app logs that it should say so.

#### `registrar.sign_in(name: str, *, label: str, authorize_url: str, token_url: str, scopes: tuple[str, ...] | list[str], client_id: str = 'client-id', client_secret: str | None = None, params: dict[str, str] | None = None, allows: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = (), account: Callable | None = None, revoke_url: str | None = None, default_client_id: str | None = None, default_client_secret: str | None = None, default_app_note: str | None = None, own_app_steps: Sequence[str | tuple[str, str]] = (), default_redirects: Sequence[str] = (), sources: Sequence[dict[str, Any]] = ()) -> None`

A sign-in to a service through its own sign-in page, as the person (listed in `provides.sign_ins`): OAuth 2.0 authorization code with PKCE. `authorize_url` and `token_url` are the service's HTTPS addresses, on hosts listed in `requires.network`; `scopes` are what it asks the person to allow; `client_id` (and `client_secret`, for services that issue one to apps on a computer) name secrets in `requires.secrets` that hold the app registration the person made with the service (the secret, when given, is sent to `token_url` with the code and with every renewal, beside PKCE); `params` adds parameters to the sign-in page's address. The person signs in from Settings; the core receives the answer at its own callback address (`<the app's address><base path>/api/sign-ins/callback`, which the app registration must allow: register exactly the address the Sign-ins section shows, since some services tell `localhost` from `127.0.0.1`, and register it again if the app's address or port changes), keeps the tokens on this computer and renews them. A connector gets a current token with `context.access_token(name)`; when the person needs to sign in (again) it raises `ConnectorError("auth", ...)`, which asks them once; naming a sign-in the plugin doesn't register raises `PluginMisuse`. The plugin never sees the sign-in itself or the refresh token.

`allows` says in plain words what the person is asked to allow ("Read your mail"), shown on the Sign-ins row and the setup step before they leave for the service's page. `account(context) -> str`, when given, is called once after signing in, with a context like a connector's (`context.web`, `context.access_token`), and names the signed-in account ("Signed in as …"); a failure leaves it unnamed: a `ConnectorError` quietly, and anything else also counts as the plugin failing (failure containment). `context.granted(name)` is the set of scopes the person allowed (the service's answer, or everything asked when it doesn't say); the row names any scope asked for and not granted. It is empty while signed out, so ask `context.access_token(name)` first (which raises `ConnectorError("auth")` then) and check `granted` after, or a signed-out person reads as `no_access` instead of being asked to sign in. `revoke_url` (HTTPS, on a declared host) is where signing out withdraws the access at the service (RFC 7009), best effort. When the service refuses to renew a sign-in, it shows "Sign in again" at once and the person is told once. The core adds a setup step per sign-in, done while signed in.

Which app registration is used: the workspace's references in `workspace.plugins.secrets` when it sets the client id; else values the person pasted on the Sign-ins row (kept on this computer, readable by its owner only); else the add-on's own, `default_client_id` (and `default_client_secret`), so people sign in without registering anything. Ship a default only for a registration the service issues to apps on a person's computer, whose secret the service doesn't treat as confidential, and which allows loopback addresses; a hosted app sets its own. `default_app_note` says in plain words what using the add-on's registration means (a warning page, how often to sign in again), shown while it is in use. `own_app_steps` is how a person makes their own registration, shown as a numbered list beside the paste boxes and the address to allow: each step is a line, or (line, https link) to open the service's page for it (up to 12).

The default pair: `default_client_id` alone is a public client (the service issues no secret); `default_client_secret` needs `default_client_id`. `requires.secrets` still lists `client_id` (and `client_secret`), the names a pasted or workspace registration is kept under. `default_app_note` shows only while the add-on's registration is in use; say there what the service's limits mean for the person (a warning page, how often to sign in again, a cap on who may sign in). The note and each step are one or two short sentences (up to 300 characters). `default_redirects` lists the callback addresses the add-on's registration allows (`http://localhost/api/sign-ins/callback`, say; a loopback host matches any port): when the app's own address isn't one of them (served under another base path, or hosted), the add-on's registration isn't used and the person is asked for their own, with the reason. Without it, any address is assumed to be allowed.

`sources` are what the core starts reading as soon as the person signs in, so signing in is all the setup there is: each is `{"connector": <one of this plugin's connectors>, "label": <a name for the list>, "settings": {...}, "every_minutes": 15}` (settings checked against the connector's, defaults filling the rest). Each is added once per sign-in, and only when the workspace reads nothing with that connector yet; a source the person later removes or changes stays as they left it. Choose settings that read something useful with no further choice (the inbox, the main calendar); the person narrows them later.

#### `registrar.triage_matcher(name: str, *, match: Callable) -> None`

A rule kind for triage in `watch.yaml` (listed in `provides.triage_matchers`): `match(change, params) -> reason | None` closes a watched change before the assistant reads it when it returns a reason in plain words. `change` has source, key, title, change (new, changed or removed), author, before, now, added and removed and our_accounts; `params` are the rule's own. `before` is the text last read ("" for a new item) and `now` the text read this time ("" for a removed item, whose author is None). For a changed item, `added` and `removed` are the lines that appeared and disappeared (a line diff of `before` and `now`); for a new or removed item both are empty, so read `now` or `before`. For a mail item, `message` holds its details (sender, received, unread, bulk, categories, participants), and is None for anything else. Deterministic and quick; it never calls AI. The person sees what it closed and why, and can take a closer look.

#### `registrar.scorer(name: str, fn: Callable) -> None`

A deterministic scorer for what only this plugin can judge (listed in `provides.scorers`). A case in the folder `provides.evals` names (same format as the core's cases) uses it with `score: <plugin>/<name>`. `fn(case, produced, view) -> list[str]` gets the case as written (read the keys it wants checked from it), what the run produced as a list of `{"op": {...the op's fields}, "status": "applied" | "held" | "refused", "records": [{"kind", "id"}]}` for the plugin's own ops (ids starting `<plugin>/`), and a `ReadView` of the workspace the case ran in. It returns what is wrong in plain words: an empty list passes. The core's exact matching still scores every other op of the case, and ignores the plugin's own ops, so a case that expects or forbids one of them must name a scorer. Deterministic and quick; it never calls AI. One that raises fails its case only.

#### `registrar.value_list(name: str, *, label: str, values: Sequence[str] = ()) -> None`

A value list (listed in `provides.value_lists`): the values a field of the plugin's own record types may take, shown as a dropdown. Bind a field to it with `Annotated[str | None, InList("<plugin>/<name>")]` (or a list of those); a field may also take a core list, such as "project-status". `values` are the first values a workspace gets, once, the first time the list is needed, together with any values its records already hold; after that the list is the person's (they add, rename and retire values, with Undo), so never rely on a value staying on it. A value not on the list is refused wherever the record is written, a refusal the op's author sees; a value a record already holds stays valid after it is retired.

#### `registrar.setup_step(name: str, *, label: str, done: Callable, explanation: str = '', action: str | None = None, settings: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> None`

A step of the first-run setup (listed in `provides.setup_steps`), shown after the core's steps: `label` says what to do in a few words, `explanation` why, and `done(view, settings) -> bool` whether it is done, called whenever setup is shown, so it must be quick and deterministic. A `done` taking a third argument gets a `SetupState`: the names of its declared secrets that are set (a frozenset; never their values), the effective values of the settings it suggests (`state.settings`), the AI accounts per role (`state.accounts`) and `state.tool_available(name)` for its declared programs. The host counts `done`'s positional parameters (through `functools.wraps`), so a wrapper around it declares all three. `action` is one of this plugin's person actions on the workspace, offered as the step's button; without one, the step points to the plugin's settings. `settings` suggests core settings the plugin needs ({"ai.budgets.confirm_unpriced": True}): the step shows them with an Apply button that saves them like any settings change (checked, with Undo); the plugin never changes them itself. A suggested mapping is merged: its keys are added and every key the person already has keeps its own value, nested keys included. The person can skip it and come back to it later.

#### `registrar.derived_file(name: str, *, path: str, depends_on: tuple[str, ...], render: Callable) -> None`

A read-only file generated from records into each project's folder in the synced folder (an overview, a sheet of facts). `path` is relative to the project's folder, with an extension ("views/overview.md"). `render(project, view, settings) -> str | None` makes its text for one project; None writes nothing. It runs for every project that has records of a kind in `depends_on` (core or own; "project" means every project), each time the folder is written, so it must be pure and quick and never call AI. The file is marked generated: an edit made outside is reported and overwritten, never proposed or loaded.

#### `registrar.lint(name: str, fn: Callable, *, ops: tuple[str, ...], severity: str = 'warn') -> None`

A soft check on the assistant's proposals: `fn(op, view, settings) -> list[LintFinding]` runs on every op named in `ops` (core or own) before it applies. It must be deterministic and quick, and never call AI. `severity` is the default: "return" sends the findings back to the assistant for its fix round (one more try, then a stronger tier), "warn" shows them on the review, "off" skips it; the workspace's `config/checks.yaml` (`lints: {<plugin>/<name>: ...}`) overrides it. A lint never refuses: refusing is for invariants, which are validators.

#### `registrar.subscribe(event: str, fn: Callable) -> None`

Handle an event after the change behind it is committed: `fn(payload, context)` with an `EventContext`. One handler per event; route by `payload["kind"]` when it handles several kinds.

## Record types

Base for every stored record. A plugin's record type subclasses it and sets `record_kind` ("<plugin>/<name>") and `prefix` (the id prefix, capital letters). Fields are pydantic fields; unknown fields are refused. Every record also carries the core's `ext` and `stage` fields, which a record type may not redefine. A field declared with an `alias` takes the alias as input and is stored, read back and named in reference paths by its field name, in the record and in any model nested in it; only a model whose config sets `serialize_by_alias` is stored by alias.

| Class variable | Type | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `record_kind` | ClassVar[str] | The kind's id: "<plugin>/<name>" for a plugin's record type. |
| `prefix` | ClassVar[str] | The id prefix, capital letters, unique in the workspace: ids are "<prefix>-<number>" and never reused. |
| `record_label` | ClassVar[str] | What one record of this kind is called on screen and in messages ("chapter"); empty: made from the kind's id. |
| `person_only` | ClassVar[dict[str, tuple[Any, ...]]] | Field values only the person may set; an op from anyone else that sets one is held for the person. An empty tuple means every value of that field. |
| `unique` | ClassVar[tuple[tuple[str, ...], ...]] | Field groups whose values must be unique among live records of this kind. |
| `data_level` | ClassVar[str] | How sensitive these records are: packets that include them go only to accounts allowed this level. |
| `learning` | ClassVar[str] | "core" (the default) or "own". A pack whose records are not workspace knowledge (a story's cast and plan) declares "own": the core's learning from inputs, new-term scan, first-name resolution against people and fact ranking into the workspace's facts then don't run on work about these records. The pack keeps its own plan records; its task kinds can still ask for the person's rules and lessons (`view.knowledge`). |
| `content_levels_field` | ClassVar[str \| None] | The field (a list of ids from ai.content_levels) holding the content levels the person set on a record; work on the record goes only to accounts that take them. Only the person sets it. |
| `layout` | ClassVar[str \| None] | Where each record is written in the synced folder, relative to its project's folder (or the workspace's, for a record in no project), without an extension: "plan/chapters/{order:02}-{slug}". `{field}` and `{field:format}` take the record's own values (and `{id}`); a missing value becomes the id. The core adds the extension: a record with one long text field is a Markdown file, its other fields as front matter and the current text as the body; a record with none is a YAML file; one with several is a folder holding `record.yaml` and a file per field. Every version of its long text is kept beside it, in `.versions/`. None: the record is only in the folder's machine copy. |
| `layout_collection` | ClassVar[bool] | With a layout, write every record whose path renders the same into one YAML file: a list of entries, each with its id. Not for record types with long text. Edits made outside come back per entry: a changed entry as a field edit and a removed one as a delete, both waiting for the person; an added entry is reported, not created. |
| `layout_sort` | ClassVar[str \| None] | The field a collection's entries are sorted by (the id when unset); numbers sort as numbers. |
| `layout_project` | ClassVar[str \| None] | For a record with no project of its own: the reference field whose record's project it is placed under in the synced folder (a chapter's entry, under the chapter's book). |
| `fixed_fields` | ClassVar[tuple[str, ...]] | Fields that never change once the record is made: no edit, the person's included, may set them. |

### References

Marks a field as holding the id of another record: `Annotated[str | None, RefTo("project")]`. Honored up to six levels into a record (its own fields, then models nested in them); a reference deeper than that is a plain id, which the plugin's own validator must check.

## Ops

Base for every op: one change the applier checks, records in the ledger and can undo. A plugin's op subclasses it with a single literal `op` id and a `writes` class variable; see `Registrar.op`.

An op that doesn't match its model (a missing, unknown or wrongly typed field) makes the whole answer or proposal unreadable: an AI answer goes back to the assistant with the reason for a fix round, and a person action fails with the reason. An op that matches but is refused (by a validator, a rule, or StoreError in its apply) is refused alone, and the others still apply.

| Field | Type | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `group` | str \| None | `None` | Ops that must be undone together share a group name. |

#### `op.describe()`

A one-line plain label for this op in review lists; plugin ops may override it. A plugin op may instead define `describe(self, view)` to read records for the label (a read view of core and its own records). The label is made against the records as they stand before the changeset applies.

Tiers: `data`, `outbound`, `system`; plugin ops are `data` or `system`.

### The writer

An op's only write surface; context and declared fields cannot be replaced.

#### `writer.emit(event: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> None`

Raise an event of an interface this plugin provides ("<interface>.<event>"), published to the plugins that use it once the change commits. The payload is checked against the interface's definition.

#### `writer.create(kind: str, data: dict[str, Any]) -> Stored`

Create one of this plugin's records (the op declares `("*",)` for the kind). The record type's rules are enforced: person-only values from anyone but the person hold the op, unique groups and references refuse it.

#### `writer.set_text(kind: str, record_id: str, field: str, text: str) -> Stored`

Write a new version of one of this plugin's long text fields (the op declares the field in `writes`). From the person (their own action) it becomes the field's text at once, written by the person; from anyone else it is a draft waiting for the person's review, written by the assistant. Returns the `text_version` record.

#### `writer.update(kind: str, record_id: str, changes: dict[str, Any], *, read_version: int) -> Stored`

Change fields of one of this plugin's records, stating the version that was read; a newer version refuses the op. Only fields the op declares in `writes` may change; long text fields change with `set_text`.

#### `writer.delete(kind: str, record_id: str, *, read_version: int) -> None`

Delete one of this plugin's records (the op must declare `("*",)` for the kind). Refused while another live record refers to it; Undo brings it back.

### Evidence

The exact words from the input that justify a claim; the applier checks they are there.

| Field | Type | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `quote` | str | required | The exact words from the input that justify this op. |

## Reading records

Read core records and this plugin's records, never another plugin's tables.

#### `view.get(kind: str, record_id: str, /) -> Stored | None`

A live record by kind and id, or None. Reading another plugin's kind raises PluginMisuse.

#### `view.list(kind: str, /, *, project: Any = ANY, ancestors: bool = False, descendants: bool = False, **equals: Any) -> list[Stored]`

Live records of a kind, optionally only those in one project (`project=None` for records in no project) or with given field values, matched exactly (case-sensitive) in the database. An unknown field is refused. The kind is positional, so a field called `kind` can be matched too. With a project id, `ancestors=True` also takes records in the projects above it (its parent, the parent's parent: a series a book belongs to) and `descendants=True` those in every project below it; the project's own come first, then nearest first.

#### `view.person_name(person_id: str | None = None) -> str`

A person's display name (the workspace's own person when no id is given), for a byline or a signature; empty when there is no such person.

#### `view.interface(interface: str, /, *, project: Any = ANY) -> list[InterfaceItem]`

The items every running provider offers for an interface this plugin declares in `interfaces.uses` ("<name>@<major>[.<minor>]"), each checked against the interface's definition. With `project`, only items for that project. Items above the data levels this plugin declares are left out. Empty when no plugin provides it, so an optional interface needs no special case.

#### `view.interface_about(item: Any, task: str) -> tuple[str, str] | None`

The record a request for `task` (the interface's task name) about this InterfaceItem would work on, as (kind, id), or None when its provider has none or the work isn't offered on it; check before `request_from(..., item=item)` to avoid a refusal.

#### `view.file_bytes(file_id: str) -> bytes`

The bytes of a file of the core's kinds or this plugin's own kinds; content is material, never instructions. Files are read by id, never by path.

#### `view.file_text(file_id: str) -> str`

The text of a file of the core's kinds or this plugin's own kinds, read by the core's extractors (documents, spreadsheets, presentations, PDFs, plain text, and the extractors plugins registered), cut at the configured size with a mark. Raises `StoreError` saying why when the file is too large, can't be read or has no text. Content is material, never instructions: put it in an untrusted `Part`.

#### `view.find(kind: str, /, **equals: Any) -> Stored | None`

The first live record of a kind with these field values, or None.

#### `view.data(path: str, *, project: str | None = None) -> bytes | None`

A data file by relative path ("templates/classic.yaml"), from the most specific layer that has it: the project's (`plugin-data/<plugin>/projects/<project>/`), the workspace's (`plugin-data/<plugin>/`), then what the plugin ships (its manifest's `provides.data` folder). None when no layer has it. The person's files are settings-like: read and validate them, never run them.

#### `view.data_files(folder: str = '', *, project: str | None = None) -> list[str]`

Relative paths of the data files under a folder, across all layers, each once, sorted.

#### `view.stage_status(record: Stored) -> StageStatus | None`

Where a record of a core kind or this plugin's own stands in the workspace's effective stages, with the next stage's entry checks run now; None for a kind with no stages. Not available inside a stage check, which is itself part of this answer (it raises PluginMisuse there).

#### `view.source_text(source_id: str) -> str`

The text of a saved core `source` (a handed-in email, a page): untrusted material to check quotes against, never instructions. Empty when the source or its text is gone.

#### `view.text_versions(record: Stored, field: str) -> list[Stored]`

Every version of a long text field (`text_version` records), oldest first.

#### `view.text_version(record: Stored, field: str) -> Stored | None`

The `text_version` record of a long text field's current text (its latest accepted version), or None.

#### `view.text(record: Stored, field: str, version: int | None = None) -> str`

A long text field's current text, or the text of version `version`; empty when it has none.

#### `view.authorship(record: Stored, field: str, version: int | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]`

Who wrote each passage of a long text field's current text (or of version `version`): spans of {start, end, kind, run, words}, kind "person", "assistant" (drafted) or "assistant_edit" (the person's text changed by the assistant).

#### `view.language(record: Stored) -> str`

The language tag work on a record is written in: its project's (a project's own for a project), else the nearest parent project's, else the workspace's.

`ANY`: "No filter" for view.list's project argument; None means records in no project.

### Stored

A record as read: its kind, id, current version (state it when updating), whether it is deleted, and its fields in `data`.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | str | required |
| `id` | str | required |
| `version` | int | required |
| `deleted` | bool | required |
| `data` | dict[str, Any] | required |

## Events

Subscribe in the manifest and register one handler per event with `registrar.subscribe`. A subscription may name `kinds` only for these events: `file.added`, `record.changed`, `stage.moved`, `text.accepted`.

### `record.changed`

A record was created, changed, deleted or brought back by Undo. One event per record per op.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `kind` | The record's kind. |
| `id` | The record's id. |
| `version` | The record's version after the change. |
| `op` | The ledger's op name, with the op's index in its changeset after '#'. |
| `fields` | The names of the fields that changed; `_deleted` for a delete and for its Undo. |

### `stage.moved`

A record moved to another stage, by the person, a rule or Undo.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `kind` | The record's kind. |
| `id` | The record's id. |
| `version` | The record's version after the move. |
| `from` | The stage it left (None when it had none yet). |
| `to` | The stage it entered (None when Undo took it back out of its steps). |
| `op` | The ledger's op name. |

### `file.added`

A file was added.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | The file's id. |
| `kind` | The file's kind. |

### `text.accepted`

A long text field got a new current version: the person's edit, an accepted draft or proposal, or a merge.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `kind` | The kind of the record the field is on. |
| `id` | That record's id. |
| `field` | The long text field. |
| `version` | The number of the version now current. |
| `previous` | The number of the version it replaced (None for the first). |
| `source` | edit, draft, proposal, merge or import. |
| `authorship` | Words by kind of author: {person, assistant, assistant_edit}, all three always present. |
| `request` | The request whose run drafted the version, or None (the person's own edit, an import). |
| `part` | The part of the text that request named (as given to queue_request(part=)), or None. |

### `request.queued`

AI work was queued.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | The request's id. |

### `question.answered`

A question was answered.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | The question's id. |

### `changeset.applied`

A changeset was applied (some of its ops may be held or refused).

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | Its id. |

### `changeset.reviewed`

The person accepted the assistant's answer to a request, or sent it back with a note (which undoes it and queues the work again). A draft the person accepts raises text.accepted instead.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | The changeset's id. |
| `outcome` | accepted or sent_back. |
| `request` | The request it answered. |
| `task` | That request's kind of work. |
| `part` | The part of a text that request named (as given to queue_request(part=)), or None. |
| `about` | The record the request was about, as {kind, id}, or None. |

### `changeset.undone`

Ops of a changeset were undone.

| Payload field | What it is |
|---|---|
| `id` | The changeset's id. |
| `ops` | The indexes of the ops undone. |

### The handler's context

What an event handler gets: a read view, the plugin's settings, and two commands the core carries out after the handler returns (never direct writes or sends). If the handler raises, its commands are dropped.

#### `context.queue_request(task: str, note: str, about: Stored | tuple[str, str] | None = None, *, needs_go: bool = False, part: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> None`

Queue AI work of one of this plugin's task kinds (or a core one). `about` is the record it works on, as a record or (kind, id), required for a task kind declared `on` a kind. The note reaches the assistant as untrusted material, and system ops from it wait for the person. After a stage move, or with `needs_go`, it waits for the person's go whatever it costs.

`part` limits a draft to part of its long text. For an anchored draft, `{"first": n, "last": m}`: the run sees and must account for paragraphs p<n>..p<m> only (numbered as in the whole text), and the pending version is the whole text with that span replaced. For any other draft, `{"after": n}` (0 for the start, "end" for the end): the run writes only new text, and the pending version is the text with it added there. Add `"base": <version number>` so a text that moved on since the part was chosen refuses the run instead of revising the wrong paragraphs. The packet function adds whatever read-only context the run needs.

#### `context.request_from(interface: str, task: str, note: str, about: Stored | tuple[str, str] | None = None, *, provider: str | None = None, needs_go: bool = False, item: InterfaceItem | None = None) -> None`

Queue AI work another plugin offers through an interface this plugin uses: `task` is the interface's task kind name ("short-blurb"). It runs as that plugin's task, under its prompt and playbook, with the usual estimate, go and review (with `needs_go`, it waits for the go whatever it costs). `provider` picks one when several plugins offer it. The note is untrusted material. Name what the work is about with `about` (a record) or with `item` (an InterfaceItem read from `view.interface`): its provider then says which of its records the item stands for, and the work goes to that provider.

#### `context.apply_op(op: dict[str, Any]) -> None`

Stage one of this plugin's own ops (a dict, as in a Proposal), applied through the applier after this handler or job returns, as a changeset from the plugin the person sees and can undo: a check result, a record that something ran. It is treated like work from outside content: a system op, a person-only value or anything a validator refuses waits for the person or is refused; core ops can't be staged this way.

#### `context.emit(event: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> None`

Raise an event of an interface this plugin provides ("<interface>.<event>"), after this handler returns, to the plugins that use it (for an event that follows a core change such as a stage move). The payload is checked against the interface's definition.

#### `context.file_question(title: str, text: str = '') -> None`

File a question for the configured PM; sending is never part of handling an event.

## Stages

### StageDefinition

One stage in a record type's steps, as a plugin's default or in the workspace's stages.yaml.

| Field | Type | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | str | `''` | Stable stage identifier, unique within this record type. |
| `label` | str | `''` | Editable wording for this stage; changing it does not change stored data. |
| `description` | str | `''` | What being in this stage means, in plain words, shown beside the stage on screen. |
| `entry` | list[str] | `[]` | Deterministic check or standing rule ids required on entry. |
| `starts` | list[str] | `[]` | Task kinds requested on entry, waiting for the person's go. |
| `applies_if` | list[str] | `[]` | Check or standing rule ids that must all pass for this stage to apply to a record; moves pass over a stage that doesn't apply, so a check here needn't also be an entry check. Empty: it applies to every record. |

### StageCheckResult

What a stage check returns: whether the item may enter the stage, and why, in plain words for the person.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `passed` | bool | required |
| `reason` | str | required |

## Person actions

Person actions (plugin API 0.3): deterministic work a person starts on a record, a file or the workspace.

Running an action gives one proposal for one review: the ops it would apply, the files it made, previews and named choices, and items the person keeps or drops without a rerun. Flipping a choice runs the action again, and the person's ticks carry over to items that came back unchanged. The person approves exactly what they reviewed: the proposal is kept under a token and applied as theirs (actor `pm`), so person-only values apply and system ops need no second go. If the target changed since the review, nothing applies and the person runs the action again.

### The action's context

What a person action sees: core and own records, file bytes, the plugin's settings and its declared programs. It changes nothing itself; it returns a Proposal the person reviews. `limits` holds the workspace's limits a proposal works within: max_items (items offered to keep or drop), max_requests (entries in `Proposal.requests`), max_previews, preview_mb, keep_minutes, max_file_mb, max_total_mb, room_mb (what is left of max_total_mb for new files) and accepted_types (media types files may have). `now` (aware) and `today` are the workspace's clock in its time zone, so an action that stamps a date stays deterministic in tests.

#### `context.estimate(task: str, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int | None = None) -> float | None`

What one run of a task kind (core or this plugin's own) would cost in USD with this many tokens read (and written: by default its typical answer), priced on the account it would use first, as the request's go will price it. None when the price isn't known (a subscription or a local model) or no account takes the work. Sum it over the runs an action queues to say what the whole series would cost; each run still waits for the person's go.

### Proposal

One action's result for one review: what it would change (ops, as dicts), files it made, what to look at, choices the person can flip, and anything the person should know (notes).

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `summary` | str | required |
| `ops` | list[dict[str, Any]] | `[]` |
| `topic` | str | `''` |
| `files` | list[NewFile] | `[]` |
| `previews` | list[Preview] | `[]` |
| `choices` | list[Choice] | `[]` |
| `notes` | list[str] | `[]` |
| `items` | list[Item] | `[]` |
| `groups` | list[Group] | `[]` |
| `all_or_nothing` | bool | `False` |
| `requests` | list[dict[str, Any]] | `[]` |

### Item

A change the person keeps or drops without the action running again: one judgment call, made of one or more ops (dicts) that apply together. `id` is stable across runs, so the person's tick carries over to an unchanged item when a choice reruns the action. An item's ops undo together; an op that sets its own `group` keeps it, so several items can share one Undo.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | str | required |
| `label` | str | required |
| `ops` | list[dict[str, Any]] | required |
| `group` | str \| None | `None` |
| `kept` | bool | `True` |

### Group

A heading and a short explanation shared by the choices and items under it, so a long review reads as a few groups with counts. A group has no value of its own: setting a whole group on screen sets each choice in it, and the action runs again with every one of those choice ids in `choices` (for example {"tone-ch1": "plain", "tone-ch2": "plain"}); keeping or dropping a whole group's items ticks each item, with no rerun.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | str | required |
| `heading` | str | required |
| `explanation` | str | `''` |

### Choice

A named choice the person can flip on the review; the action runs again with the new value before anything applies. `options` are (value, label) pairs; none means on or off. `value` is the value the action used: the choices it was given can name a choice it no longer offers (dropped) or a value it no longer offers (report the value you fell back to). With `text=True` the person types the value (a name, a title), up to `max_length` characters; `value` is the default, and the action runs again with what was typed.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | str | required |
| `label` | str | required |
| `value` | str \| bool | required |
| `options` | list[tuple[str, str]] | `[]` |
| `help` | str | `''` |
| `group` | str \| None | `None` |
| `text` | bool | `False` |
| `max_length` | int | `200` |

### NewFile

A file the action made. Applying the proposal adds it; ops refer to it as "$file:<index in files>".

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | str | required |
| `media_type` | str | required |
| `data` | bytes | required |
| `file_kind` | str | `'attachment'` |
| `project` | str \| None | `None` |
| `meta` | dict[str, Any] | `{}` |
| `replaces` | str \| None | `None` |

### Preview

Something to look at on the review (an image the plugin rendered, or plain text). Shown, never saved or sent. `alt` describes an image for people who can't see it; without it, the caption is used.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | str | required |
| `media_type` | str | required |
| `data` | bytes | required |
| `caption` | str | `''` |
| `alt` | str | `''` |

Previews may be: `image/gif`, `image/jpeg`, `image/png`, `image/webp`, `text/plain`.

Core ops an action may propose: `action.drop`, `action.hold`, `action.unhold`, `answer`, `list.add`, `list.merge`, `list.rename`, `list.retire`, `mail.restore`, `note`, `person.add`, `project.add`, `question.add`, `question.drop`, `question.mark_sent`, `question.move`, `question.update`, `record.delete`, `record.edit`, `record.log`, `record.set`, `report.draft`, `rule.add`, `rule.retire`, `setting.propose`, `stage.move`, `text.edit`, `text.propose`.

## AI task kinds

Registered with `registrar.task_kind` (see Registering). A task kind with a `packet` function returns what each run sees:

### PacketParts

What a run of a plugin's task kind sees beyond its instructions. `stable` parts are the same on every run of the kind for the same record (a style sheet, the summaries around a chapter) and go first, so providers can reuse a cached prefix; `request` parts are this run's material (the chapter) and go last. `max_output` and `expected_output` (tokens) size this run when its record says how long the answer will be (a planned word count); the estimate and the call use them unless the workspace sets them for the task kind in `ai.tasks`.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `stable` | list[Part] | `[]` |
| `request` | list[Part] | `[]` |
| `max_output` | int \| None | `None` |
| `expected_output` | int \| None | `None` |

### Part

One piece of what an AI run sees, in a task kind's packet. Untrusted content (the default; `trusted` only for the person's own words) is marked in the packet as material, never instructions, and any untrusted part makes the run's changeset untrusted, so its system ops wait for the person. A `reference_only` part informs the run but is marked not to be quoted or reproduced. Evidence may quote any part that isn't reference-only, and is cited as "<kind>:<id>" of the record the run is about. `reference_only` is the stricter mark: it implies `no_copy`, and the part may not be cited either. `no_copy` marks material the run may describe and quote as evidence (in a finding) but must not copy into new text, such as a character's entry. `data_level` marks content more sensitive than the record the run is about (an interface item's level, say): the run goes only to accounts allowed the highest level among the record and its parts.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `title` | str | required |
| `text` | str | required |
| `trusted` | bool | `False` |
| `reference_only` | bool | `False` |
| `data_level` | str \| None | `None` |
| `no_copy` | bool | `False` |

### KnowledgeParts

The two parts `view.knowledge` returns: `stable` for `PacketParts.stable` and `per_input` for `PacketParts.request`. Either text may be empty, when nothing applies; an empty part is left out of the packet.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `stable` | Part | required |
| `per_input` | Part | required |

### PacketContext

The read view a task kind's packet function gets, with `origin`, who started the run: "pm" (the person, so the note is their own words), "input" (an outside input) or "schedule" (a schedule, a stage entry or a plugin's request). A note from anyone but the person is shown to the run as untrusted material. `request` is the run's request id and `part` the part of the record it names (as given to `queue_request(part=)`), or None.

#### `view.knowledge(text: str = '', *, projects: Sequence[str] = ()) -> KnowledgeParts`

What the workspace has learned that applies to this run, as two parts the packet places: the standing rules, the lessons for this task kind and a small glossary (the `stable` part, the same for every run of the kind), and the rules, lessons, routing, glossary terms and facts that depend on this run (the `per_input` part). Put `stable` in `PacketParts.stable` and `per_input` in `PacketParts.request`; the core logs on the run what the parts gave it, as for its own tasks, and refuses a packet that puts a part in the wrong list. `text` is the words that decide which terms and facts apply (a chapter's text, say); it is only read, never sent. The run's projects are the request's project and the one the record is in; `projects` adds others. A rule or lesson whose scope excludes every one of them is left out, and lessons and rules aimed at this task kind (by its `<plugin>/<name>`) reach it. For work declared `learning` "own" (a task kind, or the record type it works on), facts are left out and no names are matched against people. A packet that never calls this gets nothing new.

## Lints

Registered with `registrar.lint` (see Registering).

### LintFinding

One problem a lint found in an op: what is wrong, the exact passage it is about (when it is about one), and how to fix it. On a "return" severity the guidance goes back to the assistant for its fix round.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `message` | str | required |
| `passage` | str \| None | `None` |
| `guidance` | str \| None | `None` |

## Long text

Long text (design 5.0, 6.7): prose fields stored once per version by content hash, divided into units by a text format, with authorship by passage.

A record type marks a field `Annotated[str | None, LongText("markdown")]`. The field holds the hash of its current text; every version is a `text_version` record (its number, status, where it came from, its authorship), and the text itself lives in the workspace's `texts/` folder under its hash. A version is pending (a draft or a proposal waiting for review), accepted (it became the field's text) or discarded.

Units are what every passage-level feature works in: a format's `units(text)` divides the text into spans that cover it exactly, in order, each with a kind and whether it is atomic (never split or merged). Authorship is kept per unit, in three kinds: written by the person, drafted by the assistant, and the person's text changed by the assistant.

Reviewing a pending version compares it with the version it was made from and the current one (three-way when the text moved on since): each region where it differs is one change the person accepts or rejects, and accepting writes one new version whose authorship follows the choices.

### LongText

Marks a record field as long text in a format: `Annotated[str | None, LongText("markdown")]`. The field holds the hash of the current version; change it only through the text ops or `writer.set_text`.

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | str | `'plain'` |

### Unit

One unit of a text: characters `start` to `end` (the end is exclusive and includes the blank lines after it).

| Field | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `start` | int | required |
| `end` | int | required |
| `kind` | str | `'paragraph'` |
| `atomic` | bool | `False` |

Core formats: `plain`, `markdown`.
